title: Insurance Fundamentals
summary: Learn how insurance works: risk pooling and premiums, key legal principles, types of life and general insurance, excesses and underinsurance, choosing and reading policies, and making honest claims.
audience: Consumers, small-business owners, finance students and new insurance staff

body.p: Insurance transfers risk. Many people each pay a relatively small, certain amount (the premium) into a pool, and the pool pays the few who suffer a covered loss. No one knows who will have a car accident or house fire this year, but insurers can estimate fairly accurately how many such events will occur across thousands of policyholders.

Suppose 1000 people each face a 2% chance of a R50 000 loss in a year. Expected claims are 1000 x 0.02 x 50 000 = R1 000 000, or R1000 per person. The insurer adds a loading for its costs, profit and uncertainty; with a 30% loading the premium is about R1300. Each person swaps a small chance of a ruinous loss for a certain, affordable cost.

list: Losses must be accidental and uncertain, not deliberate.
They must be measurable in money.
Many similar, independent risks must exist so they can be pooled.
The policyholder must have an insurable interest: they would suffer a real financial loss.

body.tip: Insure against losses you could not afford to absorb; small, predictable costs are usually cheaper to pay yourself.

body.p: Insurance contracts rest on legal principles that every policyholder should understand.

list: Utmost good faith: both sides must disclose all material facts honestly. Failing to declare, for example, a previous accident or medical condition when asked can lead to a claim being rejected.
Insurable interest: you can insure your own car or house, not a stranger's.
Indemnity: for property and liability insurance, the payout restores you to your position before the loss, not better; you should not profit from a claim.
Subrogation: after paying you, the insurer can recover the money from whoever caused the loss.
Contribution: if two policies cover the same loss, the insurers share the cost.
Proximate cause: the loss must be caused mainly by an insured event.

body.p: Life and personal-accident policies are not indemnity contracts; they pay an agreed sum because a life cannot be valued exactly.

body.tip: Answer every question on an insurance application fully and truthfully, and keep a copy.

body.p: Insurance is usually divided into life (long-term) and non-life (short-term or general) insurance.

list: Life insurance pays on death; term cover is cheaper and lasts a set period, while whole-life and endowment policies include savings.
Funeral cover pays for funeral costs; very common across Southern Africa.
Health insurance and medical schemes pay for medical treatment.
Disability and income protection replace income if you cannot work.
Motor insurance: third-party cover (damage you cause to others) and comprehensive cover (also your own car).
Property insurance: buildings and contents against fire, theft and other perils.
Business insurance: liability, business interruption, stock, goods in transit and professional indemnity.
Agricultural and microinsurance: low-cost cover for crops, livestock, health or life, often through mobile phones; index insurance pays when rainfall or yields cross a set level.

body.p: Some insurance is compulsory in many countries, such as third-party motor cover or certain workers' compensation schemes.

body.tip: Check whether your employer, bank or medical scheme already gives you some cover before buying more.

body.p: Premiums depend on the likelihood and size of possible claims. Car insurance costs more for young drivers, expensive cars and high-crime areas; life cover costs more for older people and smokers. Good risk management, such as alarms or safe driving records, can reduce premiums.

The excess is the part of each claim you pay yourself. If your car repair costs R20 000 and the excess is R2500, the insurer pays R17 500. Choosing a higher excess lowers the premium but means paying more when you claim.

If property is insured for less than its full value, many policies apply average: the payout is reduced in proportion. A house worth R800 000 insured for only R600 000 is 75% insured. After a R100 000 loss, the insurer pays 600 000 / 800 000 x 100 000 = R75 000, and the owner bears R25 000. Review sums insured regularly, especially when prices rise.

body.tip: A monthly premium of R300 costs R3600 a year; compare that with the losses it covers and the excess you would still pay.

body.p: The cheapest policy is not always the best. Compare cover, exclusions, excesses, waiting periods, claims service and the insurer's financial strength.

list: Schedule: who and what is covered, the sums insured, premium and excess.
Insured events (perils): what the policy covers.
Exclusions: what it does not cover, such as wear and tear, war, deliberate acts or pre-existing conditions.
Conditions: your duties, such as maintaining security, reporting losses promptly and paying premiums on time.
Waiting periods: time after starting before some claims are paid, common in funeral and medical cover.

body.p: Use licensed insurers and intermediaries; regulators such as South Africa's Prudential Authority and FSCA, Nigeria's NAICOM, Kenya's Insurance Regulatory Authority and Ghana's National Insurance Commission supervise them. Ask for explanations in plain language, and use the cooling-off period, if offered, to cancel a policy that does not suit you.

body.tip: Keep an inventory with photos and receipts of valuable items; it makes claims faster and helps choose the right sum insured.

body.p: When a loss happens, act quickly: protect people and property from further damage, report crimes to the police and obtain a case number, notify the insurer within the time limit, and gather evidence such as photos, receipts and witness details.

steps: Notify the insurer or broker and receive a claim number.
Complete the claim form honestly and attach evidence.
Allow assessors to inspect the damage if required.
Receive the decision; ask for reasons in writing if the claim is rejected.
If you disagree, use the insurer's complaints process, then the industry ombud or regulator.

body.p: Exaggerating claims, staging accidents or hiding facts is fraud. It is a crime, can lead to rejection of the whole claim and cancellation of cover, and pushes up premiums for everyone. Also watch for scams: fake insurance sellers, policies that do not exist, and requests to pay premiums into personal accounts.

body.tip: Pay premiums only to the insurer's official accounts or licensed intermediaries, and get written confirmation of cover.
